2. Mr Fazlur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner on behalf of the respondent No.4, submits that the election petition No.2 of 2001 is not made according to sections 50 and 51 of the aforesaid People's Order 1972. He further submits that if the election petition is not filed according to law i.e., aforesaid two Articles, it is liable to be dismissed under Article 58(a) of the People's Order 1972. He further submits that the Articles 50 & 51 is the mandatory provision for election petition and if above Article is violated; the Election Tribunal shall dismiss the election petition for non-compliance of the aforesaid Articles. He again submits that the present petition is filed against some persons who are not the candidate of the election thereby and the petitioner violated the provision of Article 50 of the People's Order, 1972. He also submits that according to Article 51(2), the petitioner may claim as relief any of the following declaration stated therein and in the petition, the petitioner prayed for many reliefs which are not according to the aforesaid Article. He submits that the petitioner violated the principle laid down in Article, 50 & 51 of the Peoples Order, 1972 in his petition and it is liable to be dismissed according to Article 58(a) of the People's Order, 1972. He further submits that prior to decide the amendment petition, the petition of the respondent No.4 shall be decided first and if the petition is found fit then amendment petition may be heard and considered and that the Civil Procedure Code is applicable when the petition is found fit for trial and not prior to that. In support of his above submission he relied on a decision reported in AIR 1969 (Supreme Court) 677; AIR 1974 (Supreme Court) 1185 and AIR 1964 (Patna) 296. 

 3. In reply to the above submission Mr Habubul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the election petitioner, submits that in the election petition, the petitioner complied with the provisions of Articles 50 & 51 of the People's Order 1972 properly and, as such, the election petition cannot be dismissed for noncompliance of the aforesaid Articles: He further submits that after compliance with the aforesaid Articles 50 & 5'1 the petitioner added some unnecessary parties as opposite party in the petition and prayed for some unnecessary prayer in, the prayer portion of the petition and by adding the unnecessary parties and prayers in the petition, it cannot be treated as not a petition under Article 49 of the People Order, 1972 and it should not be rejected in limineunder Article 58(a) of the People's Order, 1972. He again submits that all the necessary candidates of the constituency are made parties to the petition and petitioner had not left out any of the necessary parties who are required to be a party to the petition according to Article 50 of the People's Order 1972. He further submits that in the prayers portion of the petition, the petitioner prayed for the required prayer as stated in Article 51 (b) of the People's Order 1972 and with that the petitioner prayed some more prayers. He again submits that if the petitioner fails to add the necessary party as required under Article 50 and prayer as required under Article 51 (b), then the petition is liable to be rejected under Article 58(1) of the People's Order 1972. He also submits that by adding some unnecessary parties in the petition and the same redundant prayer in it, the petition cannot be called as proper petition under Article 49 of the People's Order 1972 and it should not be dismissed outright as per Article 58 of the People's Order of 1972. He against submits that during hearing, the tribunal may not look into the unnecessary parties or prayers of the election petition when there are necessary parties and requisite prayer in the petition. He submits that there is no legal bar to strike out the unnecessary parties and redundant prayers from the petition by an amendment petition under Order VI rule 17 or Order I rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the present petitioner has already filed a petition for striking out the necessary parties and redundant prayers from the election petition. In support of his above submission he relied on the decisions reported in AIR 1964 (Supreme Court) 1545 and AIR 1958, Allahabad, 858. 

 Section 86(1) ... No doubt the power of amendment is preserved to the court and Order I rule 10 enables the court to strike out parties but the court cannot use Order VI rule 17 or Order I rule 10 to avoid the consequences of non-joinder for where a special provision is to be found in the Act. The court can order an amendment and even strike out a party who is not necessary. But when the Act makes a person a necessary party and provided that the petition shall be dismissed if such a party is not joined, the power of amendment or to strike out parties cannot be used at all. The Civil Procedure Code applies subject to the provisions of the Representation of the People's Act and any rules made thereunder (see 5.87) when the Act enjoins the penalty of dismissal of the petition for non-joinder of party the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code cannot be used as curative means to save the election petition"
